lessons.title: Gender — Masculine, Feminine, Neuter
lessons.explanation: Russian nouns have three genders. Masculine nouns usually end in a consonant (стол — table, брат — brother). Feminine nouns usually end in -а or -я (книга — book, земля — earth). Neuter nouns usually end in -о or -е (окно — window, море — sea).
examples: стол (table) — masculine (ends in consonant)
книга (book) — feminine (ends in -а)
окно (window) — neuter (ends in -о)
дверь (door) — feminine (ends in soft sign ь)
lessons.tip: Nouns ending in -ь (soft sign) can be either masculine or feminine — you must memorize them.

quiz.question: What gender is 'книга' (book)?
What gender is 'окно' (window)?

lessons.title: Personal Pronouns
lessons.explanation: Russian personal pronouns: я (ya) = I, ты (ty) = you (informal), он (on) = he, она (ona) = she, оно (ono) = it, мы (my) = we, вы (vy) = you (formal/plural), они (oni) = they.
examples: Я студент. (I am a student.)
Ты мой друг. (You are my friend.)
Он говорит по-русски. (He speaks Russian.)
Мы учимся вместе. (We study together.)
lessons.tip: Use ты with friends and family; use вы with strangers, elders, and in formal situations.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I' in Russian?
Which pronoun do you use formally for 'you'?

lessons.title: No Verb 'To Be' in Present Tense
lessons.explanation: Like Arabic, Russian omits the verb 'to be' in the present tense. The subject and predicate stand next to each other with a dash sometimes used instead. Past tense uses был/была/было/были.
examples: Я студент. (I am a student.) — no verb
Это моя книга. (This is my book.)
Москва — столица России. (Moscow is the capital of Russia.) — dash
Он был врачом. (He was a doctor.) — past tense
lessons.tip: The dash is often used in written Russian to replace 'to be' when both subject and predicate are nouns.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I am a student' in Russian (present tense)?

lessons.title: Cases Introduction — Nominative and Accusative
lessons.explanation: Russian has six cases that show the role of nouns. Nominative (именительный): the subject. Accusative (винительный): the direct object. For masculine animate nouns, accusative = genitive form. For neuter nouns, accusative = nominative.
examples: Студент читает. (The student reads.) — nominative
Я вижу студента. (I see the student.) — accusative
Книга на столе. (The book is on the table.) — nominative
Я читаю книгу. (I am reading a book.) — accusative
lessons.tip: Russian has no articles (a/an/the) — meaning is determined by case endings and context.

quiz.question: How many cases does Russian have?

lessons.title: Verb Conjugation — Present Tense
lessons.explanation: Russian verbs have two conjugation types. Type I (-e conjugation): endings are -ю/-у, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют/-ут. Type II (-и conjugation): endings are -ю/-у, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят/-ат. Example читать (to read, type I): читаю, читаешь, читает, читаем, читаете, читают.
examples: Я читаю книгу. (I am reading a book.)
Ты говоришь по-английски? (Do you speak English?)
Он живёт в Москве. (He lives in Moscow.)
Мы работаем каждый день. (We work every day.)
lessons.tip: Russian verbs show who is doing the action through their ending, so subject pronouns are often omitted.

quiz.question: What ending does 'ты' take for Type I verbs?

lessons.title: Prepositional Case — Предложный падеж
lessons.explanation: The prepositional case is used only after certain prepositions, most commonly в (in) and на (on) for location, and о/об (about) for topics. Most masculine and neuter nouns add -е in this case; feminine nouns ending in -а change to -е, and those ending in -я or -ь often change to -и.
examples: Я живу в Москве. (I live in Moscow.)
Книга лежит на столе. (The book is lying on the table.)
Мы говорим о фильме. (We are talking about the movie.)
Она учится в школе. (She studies at school.)
lessons.tip: The prepositional case is the only Russian case that is never used without a preposition — that's why it's called 'prepositional'.

quiz.question: Which prepositions commonly trigger the prepositional case for location?
What is the typical ending added to masculine nouns in the prepositional case?

lessons.title: Personal Pronoun Declension
lessons.explanation: Russian personal pronouns change form depending on case, just like nouns. For example, я (I) becomes меня (accusative/genitive), мне (dative), мной (instrumental). These irregular forms must be memorized since they don't follow standard noun endings.
examples: Дай мне книгу. (Give me the book.) — dative
Я вижу его. (I see him.) — accusative
Она пошла со мной. (She went with me.) — instrumental
У меня есть кот. (I have a cat. [lit. 'By me there is a cat']) — genitive
lessons.tip: Pronoun case forms are highly irregular, so drill them as a fixed set (я/меня/мне/мной) rather than trying to derive them from rules.

quiz.question: What is the dative case form of я (I)?
Which case form of я is used in 'У меня есть...' (I have...)?

lessons.title: Plural Formation of Nouns
lessons.explanation: In the nominative case, most Russian masculine and feminine nouns form the plural by adding -ы or -и (depending on the final consonant/spelling rule). Neuter nouns typically change -о to -а or -е to -я. Some nouns have irregular plurals that must be memorized.
examples: стол → столы (table → tables)
книга → книги (book → books)
окно → окна (window → windows)
друг → друзья (friend → friends, irregular)
lessons.tip: After velar consonants (г, к, х) and hushing sounds (ж, ш, ч, щ), spelling rules require -и instead of -ы.

quiz.question: What is the plural of 'книга' (book)?
How do most neuter nouns ending in -о form their plural?

lessons.title: Aspect — Perfective and Imperfective
lessons.explanation: Russian verbs come in pairs: imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) and perfective (completed/one-time action). Example: читать (imperfective, to read/be reading) vs. прочитать (perfective, to read/finish reading). Aspect is a fundamental feature of Russian grammar.
examples: Я читал книгу. (I was reading a book.) — imperfective
Я прочитал книгу. (I read/finished the book.) — perfective
Он всегда пишет письма. (He always writes letters.) — imperfective
Он написал письмо. (He wrote a letter.) — perfective
lessons.tip: Think of imperfective as the 'movie' (process) and perfective as the 'photo' (completed result).

quiz.question: Which aspect describes a completed action?

lessons.title: Past Tense Formation and Gender Agreement
lessons.explanation: Russian past tense verbs are formed by removing -ть from the infinitive and adding -л (masculine), -ла (feminine), -ло (neuter), or -ли (plural), agreeing with the subject's gender and number rather than the person. There is no distinction for 1st/2nd/3rd person in the past tense.
examples: Он читал книгу. (He was reading/read a book.) — masculine
Она читала книгу. (She was reading/read a book.) — feminine
Мы читали книгу. (We read a book.) — plural
Окно было открыто. (The window was open.) — neuter
lessons.tip: Since Russian past tense agrees with gender/number, not person, 'я читал' vs 'я читала' tells you the speaker's gender.

quiz.question: What ending does a past tense verb take with a feminine subject?
Does Russian past tense distinguish 1st/2nd/3rd person?
options: No, it agrees with gender and number instead

lessons.title: Motion Verbs — идти/ходить, ехать/ездить
lessons.explanation: Russian has paired motion verbs distinguishing unidirectional (one specific trip, one direction) from multidirectional (habitual, round-trip, or general ability) movement. идти (unidirectional, on foot) vs ходить (multidirectional, on foot); ехать (unidirectional, by vehicle) vs ездить (multidirectional, by vehicle).
examples: Я иду в школу. (I am going to school [right now, on foot].) — unidirectional
Я хожу в школу каждый день. (I go to school every day.) — multidirectional
Мы едем в Москву. (We are driving to Moscow [right now].) — unidirectional
Он часто ездит в Москву. (He often travels to Moscow.) — multidirectional
lessons.tip: Ask: is this a single trip happening now/soon (unidirectional) or a repeated/habitual/round-trip (multidirectional)?

quiz.question: Which verb describes a single, one-direction trip on foot happening now?
Which verb would you use for 'I go to school every day' (on foot)?

lessons.title: Dative and Instrumental Cases
lessons.explanation: The dative case marks the indirect object ('to/for whom') and is used with verbs like давать (to give) and нравиться (to like/please), plus prepositions like к (toward) and по (along/according to). The instrumental case marks the means or instrument ('by/with what') and is used with с (with) for accompaniment, and after verbs like быть (to be) in some constructions.
examples: Я дал книгу другу. (I gave the book to my friend.) — dative
Мне нравится музыка. (I like music. [lit. 'Music is pleasing to me']) — dative
Я пишу ручкой. (I write with a pen.) — instrumental
Она пошла с другом. (She went with a friend.) — instrumental
lessons.tip: The dative answers 'to/for whom?' while the instrumental answers 'by/with what means?' — keep the two questions separate to choose correctly.

quiz.question: Which case is used for the indirect object ('to whom')?
Which preposition commonly triggers the instrumental case for accompaniment?

lessons.title: Declension of Adjectives
lessons.explanation: Russian adjectives must agree with the noun in gender, number, and case. Each adjective has multiple forms. Masculine nominative singular: -ый/-ий/-ой. Feminine nominative singular: -ая/-яя. Neuter nominative singular: -ое/-ее. Plural nominative: -ые/-ие.
examples: новый дом (a new house — masc.)
новая книга (a new book — fem.)
новое окно (a new window — neut.)
новые слова (new words — plural)
красивая девушка (a beautiful girl)
lessons.tip: Once you know the noun's gender, number, and case, you can predict the adjective ending.

quiz.question: What ending does a masculine adjective take in nominative singular?

lessons.title: Aspect in the Imperative and Infinitive
lessons.explanation: Verbal aspect choice matters even outside past/future tense. In positive commands, perfective aspect is typical for a single specific request, while imperfective is used for general invitations or repeated actions. Negative commands almost always use imperfective aspect, even for a one-time prohibition, to soften the command.
examples: Закрой дверь! (Close the door! — perfective, specific one-time request)
Закрывай дверь, когда выходишь. (Close the door [each time] when you leave. — imperfective, habitual)
Не закрывай дверь! (Don't close the door! — imperfective negative command)
Не забудь позвонить. (Don't forget to call. — imperfective negative + perfective infinitive)
lessons.tip: When in doubt with negative commands, default to imperfective aspect — it is the standard choice for prohibitions in Russian.

quiz.question: Which aspect is typically used for negative commands, even one-time prohibitions?
options: neither, a different mood is used

quiz.question: Which aspect is typical for a single specific positive command?

lessons.title: Participles — Причастия
lessons.explanation: Russian participles (причастия) are verbal adjectives that describe a noun by an action. There are four types: present active (-ущий/-ющий/-ащий/-ящий), past active (-вший/-ший), present passive (-емый/-имый), and past passive (-нный/-тый/-енный). They decline like adjectives, agreeing in gender, number, and case.
examples: читающий студент (a reading student) — present active
прочитавший книгу студент (the student who read the book) — past active
читаемая книга (the book being read) — present passive
прочитанная книга (the book that has been read) — past passive
lessons.tip: Participles let you compress a relative clause ('the student who is reading') into a single adjective-like word — common in written/formal Russian.

quiz.question: What does a present active participle describe?
options: a noun currently performing an action
a noun that already finished an action
a noun receiving an action now

quiz.question: How do participles behave grammatically?

lessons.title: Verbal Adverbs — Деепричастия
lessons.explanation: Verbal adverbs (деепричастия) describe an action happening alongside the main verb's action, similar to English '-ing' clauses ('while doing...'). Imperfective verbal adverbs are formed with -я/-а from the present stem (simultaneous action). Perfective verbal adverbs are formed with -в/-вши/-ши from the past stem (completed action before the main action).
examples: Читая книгу, он пил чай. (While reading a book, he drank tea.) — imperfective, simultaneous
Закончив работу, она пошла домой. (Having finished work, she went home.) — perfective, prior action
Улыбаясь, она поздоровалась. (Smiling, she said hello.) — imperfective
Открыв дверь, он вошёл. (Having opened the door, he entered.) — perfective
lessons.tip: Unlike participles, verbal adverbs never decline — they are invariable, functioning like adverbs rather than adjectives.

quiz.question: What does a perfective verbal adverb typically express relative to the main verb?
options: an action completed before the main action

quiz.question: Do verbal adverbs (деепричастия) decline for gender, number, or case?
